title: Ali Fazal Hunts Two Killers Across 1970s Delhi. Sonali Bendre Plays the Mother Left Behind.
excerpt: Prime Video's Raakh drops all eight episodes tomorrow — a true-crime-inspired thriller that reunites the Paatal Lok director with an extraordinary cast, streaming in 240+ countries
body:
The trailer opens on a pair of eyes. Not wide with surprise — narrowed, calculating, almost amused. Then a laugh, low and unhinged, cuts through the silence. Within seconds, you know this isn't a typical whodunit. This is a hunt.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=RdB_TgwLPqs

Raakh, Prime Video's new eight-episode series premiering June 12, is set in 1978 Delhi — a city still naive enough to be stunned by a crime this violent. Two teenagers vanish. A family shatters. And a young Sub-Inspector named Jayprakash, played by Ali Fazal, launches a manhunt that will pull him into places darker than any case file could prepare him for.

The series is inspired by the infamous Ranga-Billa case — one of the most shocking criminal episodes in Indian history. In 1978, two siblings were kidnapped in broad daylight from a bus stop in South Delhi by Kuljeet Singh (Ranga) and Jasbir Singh (Billa). The nationwide manhunt, trial, and eventual execution of the two men became a turning point in India's criminal justice conversation. It was the kind of case that changed how an entire generation thought about safety in the capital.

Raakh fictionalises this story through the characters of Babu (Akash Makhija) and Rajjo (Ramandeep Yadav), two men whose violence is rooted in damage the show takes its time revealing. The trailer intercuts their crimes with flashes of their childhoods — the series clearly has no interest in making them monsters and moving on. It wants you to understand what made them, even as it refuses to excuse them.

"What stays with you from great crime stories is rarely just the crime or the investigation. You remember the deeply human emotions." — creators Anusha Nandakumar and Sandeep Saket

On the other side of the investigation stands Sonali Bendre, playing one of the teenagers' parents. For anyone who grew up watching Bendre in the 90s — in Sarfarosh, Hum Saath-Saath Hain, Diljale — her return to serious dramatic work carries its own emotional weight. This is a woman who battled metastatic cancer publicly in 2018, documented her treatment in New York, and came back not to reclaim stardom but to choose roles with intention. In Raakh, she carries the grief that drives the story forward. Aamir Bashir plays opposite her as the father, adding another layer of credibility to a cast that clearly wasn't assembled for marquee value alone.

Director Prosit Roy knows how to make streaming crime feel cinematic. He was behind the camera for Paatal Lok, the Amazon series that redefined Indian noir for a global audience, and Pari, the Anushka Sharma horror film that proved the streaming aesthetic could translate to theatres. With Raakh, Roy is working from a script by Anusha Nandakumar and Sandeep Saket, who also co-directed episodes, with dialogue by Ayush Trivedi. The pedigree is serious.

But the real casting coup is Fazal. Since Mirzapur made him a household name, the actor has built a parallel international career — Furious 7, Victoria & Abdul opposite Judi Dench, and Kenneth Branagh's Death on the Nile. He's one of a handful of Indian actors who can open a show for both domestic and global audiences simultaneously. In Raakh, he plays a cop for what appears to be the first time — a young officer who starts methodical and becomes increasingly consumed by the chase.

The visual texture of the trailer is worth noting. 1970s Delhi has been recreated with the kind of muted, golden palette that suggests cigarette smoke and Ambassador cars and newspapers folded on tea stalls. There are no neon-lit interrogation rooms here. The period detail feels lived-in rather than production-designed, which is exactly the tone a show like this needs.

The supporting cast rounds out the ensemble with names that signal depth: Rakesh Bedi, the veteran comic actor in what appears to be a rare dramatic role, Dibyendu Bhattacharya (who was unforgettable in Paatal Lok), and Anshul Chauhan. The show is produced by Endemol Shine India in association with BhaDiPa — the same Marathi digital content studio that proved regional storytelling could scale.

Where to Watch — and Why Diaspora Viewers Should Care

All eight episodes of Raakh drop at midnight IST on June 12, streaming on Amazon Prime Video in Hindi across 240+ countries and territories. That's a simultaneous global release — no waiting weeks for an international window.

For NRI audiences, the Ranga-Billa case occupies a specific place in cultural memory. It's the case your parents or grandparents reference when they talk about how Delhi changed. It's been adapted before — the 2013 Telugu film Ranga The Donga touched on it — but never with this level of production value or this calibre of cast. Raakh isn't just a true-crime dramatisation. It's an attempt to understand what violence does to a city, a family, and the people tasked with making it stop.

The creators have been clear: this is not a procedural. "From the very beginning, we weren't interested in building a world that revolved solely around the mystery," Nandakumar and Saket said. "We wanted to create a holistic emotional landscape — one that explored grief, guilt, love, anger, and the ways in which a single act can ripple through the lives of everyone it touches."

That's a promising mandate. Whether Raakh delivers on it will depend on how well it balances the thriller mechanics with the human cost. But with this cast, this director, and this source material, the pieces are in place for something genuinely excellent.
